clinicalScope: Insulin hormone physiology and its clinical implications in adult and paediatric patients in low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Insulin Physiology and Clinical Reasoning
subject: Physiology
summary: Insulin is a peptide hormone that lowers blood glucose by moving sugar into cells. It also controls fat and protein metabolism, and its deficiency or excess drives diabetes and related emergencies.

sections.p: Insulin, secreted by pancreatic β‑cells, is the chief anabolic hormone that maintains glucose homeostasis by promoting cellular uptake and storage of glucose, while inhibiting hepatic glucose production.
b: Produced as pro‑insulin → cleaved to A (21 aa) and B (30 aa) chains linked by disulfide bonds.
Normal fasting plasma insulin: 5–20 µU/mL; post‑prandial peaks up to 80 µU/mL.
Works with glucagon (α‑cell hormone) in a yin‑yang balance.
Key target organs: liver, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue.
Deficiency → hyperglycaemia (type 1, advanced type 2, pancreatic loss).
Excess (iatrogenic) → hypoglycaemia, especially after re‑feeding.

sections.p: After a carbohydrate meal, glucose rises → β‑cell depolarisation → calcium influx → insulin granule exocytosis.
b: Glucose enters β‑cell via GLUT2 (high Km).
ATP generated closes K‑ATP channels, depolarising membrane.
Voltage‑gated Ca²⁺ channels open, triggering insulin release.
Insulin enters portal circulation, first‑pass liver uptake (~50%).
Peak insulin within 30–60 min, return to baseline in 2–3 h.

sections.p: Insulin binds the insulin receptor (a tyrosine kinase) initiating cascades that translocate GLUT4 transporters and modulate metabolic enzymes.
b: Receptor autophosphorylation → IRS‑1/2 recruitment.
PI3K‑Akt pathway → GLUT4 vesicle fusion in muscle/fat.
Akt phosphorylates glycogen synthase kinase‑3 → activates glycogen synthase.
Inhibits hormone‑sensitive lipase → reduces lipolysis.
Stimulates protein synthesis via mTOR.

sections.p: Insulin secretion is tightly coupled to nutrient signals and modulated by autonomic and hormonal inputs.
b: Stimulators: ↑ glucose, ↑ amino acids (especially leucine), incretins (GLP‑1, GIP), parasympathetic acetylcholine.
Inhibitors: ↑ catecholamines, somatostatin, cortisol, growth hormone.
Negative feedback: hyperglycaemia → insulin rise → glucose fall → insulin decline.
In fasting, low insulin permits glucagon‑driven gluconeogenesis.

sections.p: Insulin coordinates liver, muscle and adipose metabolism to store excess energy and spare glucose for the brain.
b: Liver: ↑ glycogen synthesis, ↓ gluconeogenesis, ↓ VLDL secretion.
Muscle: ↑ GLUT4 translocation, ↑ glycogen storage, ↑ protein synthesis.
Adipose: ↑ lipogenesis, ↓ lipolysis, ↑ fatty acid uptake.
Kidney: contributes to peripheral glucose uptake; insulin resistance may affect renal sodium handling.

sections.p: Various physiological and pathological conditions modify insulin action, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Pregnancy → insulin resistance (↑ placental hormones).
Infection (malaria, HIV, TB) → cytokine‑mediated resistance.
Malnutrition → β‑cell exhaustion, blunted secretion.
Herbal remedies (e.g., bitter leaf) may contain insulin‑like peptides.
Physical activity → insulin‑independent GLUT4 uptake, improving sensitivity.

sections.p: Failure of insulin secretion or action underlies diabetes mellitus and acute metabolic crises.
b: Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune β‑cell destruction → absolute insulin deficiency.
Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance + relative β‑cell failure; common with obesity, HIV‑ART, chronic infections.
Re‑feeding syndrome: sudden insulin surge drives potassium, phosphate, magnesium into cells → severe hypokalaemia.
Insulinoma (rare): autonomous secretion → fasting hypoglycaemia.
Iatrogenic overdose: excess exogenous insulin → neuroglycopenic symptoms.

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the direction of glucose imbalance and the metabolic shift caused by insulin.
b: Deficiency: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, ketoacidosis (acetone breath, abdominal pain).
Resistance: gradual hyperglycaemia, fatigue, blurred vision.
Excess: sweating, tremor, confusion, seizures, coma (blood glucose < 3 mmol/L).
Re‑feeding: muscle weakness, arrhythmia from hypokalaemia.

sections.p: Laboratory tests confirm insulin status and guide acute management.

t.b: Is the patient hyper‑ or hypoglycaemic? ≥ 11.1 mmol/L suggests diabetes; ≤ 3.0 mmol/L indicates hypoglycaemia.
High with low glucose → insulinoma or exogenous overdose; low with high glucose → β‑cell failure.
Distinguishes endogenous vs exogenous insulin; low in type 1, high in insulinoma.
Detect re‑feeding shifts; K⁺ < 3.3 mmol/L warrants correction before insulin infusion.
Rapid bedside glucose; essential where labs are delayed.

sections.p: Understanding insulin physiology directs acute and chronic management in low‑resource settings.
b: DKA: give IV fluids, correct K⁺, start regular insulin infusion 0.1 U/kg/h after first fluid bolus.
Re‑feeding: start low‑dose insulin (0.05 U/kg) when electrolytes are ≥ 3.3 mmol/L K⁺, monitor electrolytes q4‑6 h.
Type 2 diabetes: lifestyle first; metformin preferred, insulin added when HbA1c > 9 % or symptomatic.
Insulin storage: keep vials away from heat; in tropical climates use cool boxes.

sections.p: Clarify frequent errors that can mislead clinicians.
b: “Insulin always lowers potassium” – true only when glucose falls; rapid shifts can cause severe hypokalaemia.
“All diabetics need insulin” – many type 2 patients achieve control with oral agents.
“Glucose‑only monitoring is enough” – ignoring electrolytes in re‑feeding leads to arrhythmia.
“Insulin works only after meals” – muscle contraction can uptake glucose independently.

sections.p: Strategic thinking for ward‑round and viva questions.
b: Always assess glucose, electrolytes, and mental status before starting insulin.
When faced with hypoglycaemia, ask: is it endogenous (insulinoma) or exogenous?
In DKA, prioritize fluid resuscitation, then potassium, then insulin.
If a test (C‑peptide) is unavailable, infer endogenous insulin by clinical context and glucose trends.

whenToSeekHelp: Unconscious patient with blood glucose < 2.5 mmol/L
Severe electrolyte derangement (K⁺ < 2.5 mmol/L) before insulin

faq.q: Why does exercise improve insulin sensitivity?
faq.a: Muscle contraction translocates GLUT4 to the membrane without insulin, reducing the amount needed for glucose uptake.

faq.q: Can insulin be given subcutaneously in DKA?
faq.a: In low‑resource settings IV may be unavailable; sub‑Q regular insulin every 1–2 h can be used, but monitor glucose closely.

faq.q: What is the role of the C‑peptide test?
faq.a: C‑peptide is co‑secreted with insulin; it remains detectable after exogenous insulin, helping differentiate endogenous from exogenous sources.

exam: A 7‑year‑old with new‑onset type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting and glucose 28 mmol/L – what is the immediate management priority? — Correct potassium first, then start insulin infusion.

A malnourished adult is started on high‑carb feeds; after 12 h glucose is 6 mmol/L but potassium falls to 2.8 mmol/L – what explains this? — Re‑feeding syndrome: insulin‑driven intracellular shift of K⁺.

How does insulin resistance in pregnancy differ from that in obesity? — Pregnancy resistance is driven by placental hormones (hPL, estrogen) and is transient; obesity resistance is chronic, linked to adipokines and inflammation.

A patient on sulfonylurea develops hypoglycaemia; why might measuring C‑peptide be useful? — To determine if endogenous insulin is still being secreted; low C‑peptide suggests overdose rather than insulinoma.
Explain why a patient with DKA may have a normal serum potassium despite total body depletion. — Insulin deficiency and acidosis shift K⁺ out of cells, masking depletion.
In a rural clinic without insulin assays, how would you differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes? — Look for rapid onset, weight loss, ketoacidosis, age < 30, and absence of obesity.
Why is it unsafe to give insulin before confirming serum potassium ≥ 3.3 mmol/L? — Insulin drives K⁺ into cells, precipitating severe hypokalaemia and arrhythmia.

What is the physiological basis for the ‘glucose‑insulin clamp’ technique? — It maintains a constant insulin infusion while adjusting glucose infusion to keep plasma glucose steady, measuring insulin sensitivity.
A patient on high‑dose steroids develops hyperglycaemia; which insulin regimen is most appropriate initially? — Start basal‑bolus with short‑acting insulin before meals, adjusting for steroid timing.

Describe the sequence of events leading from β‑cell depolarisation to insulin granule exocytosis. — Glucose ↑ → ATP ↑ → K‑ATP channels close → membrane depolarises → Ca²⁺ influx → insulin granules fuse with membrane.
